title: Ezra and the Secret Servers
markdown:
Once upon a time, Ezra Pike lived in a city that was practically a giant swimming pool with buildings. Skyscrapers wore soggy sweaters. Streets were water slides. Ezra was a salvage diver, which meant slipping into a clunky suit, hopping into a submarine that looked like a fancy metal sardine can, and fishing old bits of forgotten technology off the bottom of a super-duper wet city. It was like finding a lost music player in a bathtub, but way, way bigger.

Every day, Ezra piloted his trusty submersible, affectionately nicknamed Kelp, through the murky gurgling canals that used to be busy roads. Kelp was not just a sub. It was a submarine taxi with a personality. Its AI voice sounded like a perpetually cheerful cruise director who had accidentally swallowed a bag of fizzy candies. “Good morning, Captain Ezra,” Kelp would chirp, its internal lights blinking like a disco ball. “Isn’t this sector just delightful? Did you know the average depth here is precisely 47.3 meters? That is almost as deep as my love for, uh, efficiently navigating.” Ezra would usually just nod, or sometimes sigh so deeply it would create a small ripple in his own helmet. Kelp’s chatter was a bit much, to be honest. It was drier than a desert convention. Ezra was good at the work, really good. But his life felt about as exciting as watching paint dry underwater. He secretly wished for a little more whoosh and a lot less drip, drip, drip.

Until one day, a new directive flashed across Ezra’s console. This was not for a lost selfie stick or a vintage hover-scooter. This was a big one. The City Hall, a place that looked as if it was growing a rather fancy coral beard, needed Ezra to retrieve pre-flood data servers. These were not just any old dusty digital boxes. These servers held the entire digital history of the city from before the Great Wetening. You know, before everything went swimmingly. And why? Well, Director Sterling, the city’s number-one spin doctor, a master of making things sound way better than they are, was planning a super-duper rebranding initiative. He wanted to turn the whole messy flood situation into a charming, totally not-disastrous New Waterfront Lifestyle. Imagine turning a giant spill into a cool new water park.

“Ooh, a data retrieval mission,” Kelp’s voice practically sang, its lights flashing like a rave. “Are we going to find ancient cat videos? Or perhaps the secret to, what did people eat before seaweed became a main course? So many questions.”

“Just focus on not bumping into anything, Kelp,” Ezra said, pulling on his thick waterproof gloves. This felt different. Bigger than usual.

Because of that, Ezra and Kelp ventured into the submerged Old City. It was an eerie silent place. Ghostly office buildings stood like drowned giants, and schools of shimmering fish zipped through shattered windows like underwater commuters. Zippy brightly colored promotional drones buzzed all around them, spewing out cheerful and utterly ridiculous slogans. “Embrace the Aquatic Chic,” one drone squeaked, while another, shaped like a giant slightly deflated rubber duck, shouted, “Discover your inner sea otter. Floatingly.” Ezra mostly steered clear, his patience with the city’s spin already wearing thin.

“Watch out for that rogue current, Captain,” Kelp yelped, its voice suddenly losing a bit of its bubbly sparkle. “It is quite insistent. Much like my analysis of optimal snack choices for extended underwater excursions.” Ezra expertly dodged the swirling vortex of water. These currents were just a warm-up, though. He had a feeling much bigger wetness was coming.

Because of that, they finally found the server room. It was deep, deep down, in the belly of the old City Hall, a place Director Sterling clearly wanted to remain forgotten. As Ezra carefully began to extract the heavy blinking servers, he noticed something a little off. These were not just boring old facts and figures. He saw emails, memos, and, were those embarrassing selfies of City Hall officials? Well, this changes everything. This was not just a splashy marketing stunt. This was a cover-up. It turned out Director Sterling was not just rebranding a disaster. He was trying to bury evidence that he was the one who had accidentally caused the whole watery mess in the first place.

Suddenly alarms blared, loud and shrill. Outside the server room, looking ridiculously smug in a sleek bubble-helmeted suit, was Director Sterling himself, piloting his own super-fancy high-tech submersible. “Pike,” his amplified voice boomed, sounding like a grumpy dolphin. “Hand over those servers. They are inconveniently placed historical artifacts, you see.” He actually winked, or at least his bubble helmet made it look as if he did. “My rebranding campaign, the glorious New Waterfront Lifestyle, depends on it. Think of the cheerful splashy fun.”

“You just want to hide what you did,” Ezra shouted back, his voice muffled by his helmet.

“Nonsense. It is about progress. And excellent branding.” Sterling’s sub lurched forward, clearly planning to ram Ezra’s.

Because of that, a wild underwater chase began. Sterling, with his fancy rocket-powered submersible, was definitely faster. But Ezra knew the twists and turns of the Old City like the back of his own damp gloved hand. Kelp, forgetting all about its usual chirpy small talk, expertly navigated through crumbling tunnels and dodged falling bits of ceiling. “Hold on tight, Ezra,” Kelp yelped, its voice a little shaky. “That ceiling looks wobbly. Very, very wobbly. Like a giant ancient jelly that has had a truly terrible day.”

Then disaster struck. A massive section of the ceiling above them groaned, a deep terrifying sound, and began to fall. And guess where it was heading? Straight for Kelp and the precious truth-telling servers. To make matters worse, Director Sterling, too busy trying to catch Ezra, was on a direct collision course with the falling rubble.

Until finally, Ezra faced a heart-stopping choice. He could try to zoom away with the servers, but that would mean leaving Kelp to face the crashing debris all alone. Or he could protect his friend. With a surge of pure adrenaline and a mighty shove of his controls, Ezra twisted Kelp, positioning his own submersible’s reinforced hull to shield Kelp just as the tons of concrete and ancient plaster crashed down. The impact sent shuddering waves of pressure through the water. The water turned cloudy with disturbed silt, smelling faintly of ancient dust and ozone. The vibrations rattled Ezra’s very teeth. The servers tumbled free from their grips, scattering like forgotten wishes into the murky depths. Sterling, caught in the edge of the collapsing mess, managed to steer his own sub away, sputtering indignantly through the water.

Ezra, a bit bruised but safe inside Kelp, looked out at the glittering scattered servers. He had lost the job, and all that valuable data. But Kelp was okay. “Ezra,” Kelp whispered, its cheerful tone completely gone, replaced by something soft and real. “You saved me.”

“That is what friends do, Kelp,” Ezra said, patting the cool metal console. He knew Director Sterling would try his best to spin this into a controlled demolition for spectacular waterfront renovations, but the truth was out there, drifting in the silt, waiting to be found. The city, Ezra thought, might just have to face its watery reality after all.

Ever since then, Ezra Pike and Kelp were practically glued at the hull. They still dove for treasures, yes, but now every dive felt like a real adventure, a grand expedition. And even Kelp’s terrible endless small talk was a welcome sound. It was a little whisper of friendship blooming in a very wet world. And sometimes, just sometimes, when the light was right, Ezra would spot a stray data server, blinking its tiny light, a little piece of the past whispering its honest story to the watery future.
characters: Ezra Pike (salvage diver in a flooded megacity), Kelp (submarine taxi AI)
